prayer.text: Pope Saint Gregory VII, pray for us.

cues.text: A Humble Beginning
Hildebrand was born between 1020 and 1025 near Soana in Tuscany, to a humble family.
As a boy he went to Rome to be educated at the monastery of Santa Maria on the Aventine, where his uncle Laurentius was abbot.
He became a Benedictine monk at Rome.
The house was marked by the austere spirit of Cluny, the great reforming abbey of the age.
He served John Gratian, who became Pope Gregory VI, and followed him into exile at Cologne in 1046.
When Gregory VI died there in 1047, Hildebrand withdrew to Cluny for more than a year.
Servant of Many Popes
In 1049 Hildebrand returned to Rome with Bruno, Bishop of Toul, who had become Pope Leo IX.
Leo made him a cardinal-subdeacon and gave him charge of the Patrimony of Saint Peter.
Nicholas II made him archdeacon in 1059, and he helped shape that year's decree on papal elections.
Under Alexander II he served as chancellor of the Apostolic See, among the most influential men at the papal court.
A Reluctant Pope
Alexander II died on April 21, 1073.
The clergy and people of Rome acclaimed Hildebrand as his successor, and the cardinals elected him in the church of San Pietro in Vincoli.
The decree of election, dated April 22, called him a man "firm in adversity and temperate in prosperity."
He protested the choice.
He took the name Gregory.
Henry IV, the German king, approved the election, the last papal election an emperor ever ratified.
Gregory was ordained a priest and consecrated on June 29, 1073, the feast of Saints Peter and Paul.
Cleansing the Church
Gregory set himself against two great evils.
One was simony, the buying and selling of Church offices.
The other was the failure of clergy to keep their vow of chastity.
At his first Lenten synod, in March 1074, he decreed that clergy who had bought their orders or offices must stop ministering, and that the sale of Church rights was forbidden.
His decrees met fierce resistance in Italy, Germany, and France.
He also condemned lay investiture, the ceremony in which a king gave a bishop his ring and staff.
A Roman synod excommunicated anyone, even an emperor or a king, who conferred such an investiture.
A list of twenty-seven propositions entered in his register in 1075, the Dictatus Papae, sets out his view of papal authority.
Scholars debate who composed it, but it expresses his principles.
Canossa
Henry IV would not yield.
In January 1076 he and most of the German bishops met at Worms and renounced obedience to Gregory, addressing him only as "Brother Hildebrand."
Gregory answered at his Lenten synod in February.
He deposed and excommunicated Henry and released his subjects from their oaths of loyalty.
Henry then crossed the Alps and came to Canossa, where Gregory was staying.
In his own letter to the German princes, Gregory wrote that Henry stood three days before the gate, "with bare feet and clad in wool."
Countess Matilda of Tuscany and Abbot Hugh of Cluny interceded for him.
On January 28, 1077, Gregory loosed the anathema and received Henry back into communion.
He asked only that Henry submit to a future council.
Exile at Salerno
The German princes elected Rudolf of Swabia as a rival king on March 15, 1077.
Henry renewed the struggle, and in 1080 Gregory excommunicated him a second time.
That June, Henry's supporters at Brixen declared Gregory deposed and chose Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, as antipope Clement III.
On March 21, 1084, Henry entered Rome, and Guibert crowned him emperor.
Gregory's ally Robert Guiscard then advanced on the city with his Normans, and Henry withdrew.
The Romans turned against the Normans' excesses, and Gregory left the city.
He went first to Monte Cassino and then to Salerno.
He died there on May 25, 1085.
His last words, as tradition records them, echo the Psalms: "I have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore I die in exile."
Legacy
The movement of renewal that took his name, the Gregorian reform, remains his best-known work.
At Salerno in 1985, on the nine hundredth anniversary of his death, Pope John Paul II said that Gregory loved the Church, the bride of Christ, and wanted her pure, chaste, holy, and free.
We see in Gregory a man who would accept exile rather than yield the freedom of the Church.
Gregory XIII beatified him in 1584, and Benedict XIII canonized him in 1728.
His life asks every believer a hard question: what are we willing to lose in order to stay faithful?
